CLIP gains come from short, discriminative tokens (counts, canonical object names, colors, numbers, visible text) placed early and unambiguous — the prompt doesn’t force these strongly enough.  
- It also leaves ambiguity about which facts are mandatory vs optional, how to treat role words, what counts as a “fact,” and how to avoid hallucinating text or roles.

Concrete, actionable feedback to change the prompt (what to change and why)

1) Make mandatory, machine-checkable requirements
- Change vague guidance into rules the model can follow deterministically: require (A) legible text exact transcription if clearly readable OR explicitly omit text, (B) if a prominent object/person is present, include an exact count and canonical object noun, and (C) include at least one color/marking or equipment token for counted objects when visible.  
- Why: CLIP strongly rewards presence of these tokens; making them mandatory increases discriminative signal.

2) Define “prominent” and “fact” and enforce 2–6 facts precisely
- Add a one-line definition: “Prominent = occupies meaningful area or center focus; a fact = one discrete visual property (count/object type/color/pose/relative placement/light).” Require 2–6 such facts and make them distinct.  
- Why: prevents filler words and ensures the model actually supplies discriminative tokens rather than long descriptions.

3) Force canonical nouns and numeric tokens, early in the sentence
- Insist on canonical object names (bicycle, pedicab/pedicab/rickshaw, goal/net, sculpture) and numerals (prefer digits: “2 people” or “3 bicycles”) placed near the start of the sentence.  
- Why: CLIP alignment improves when the caption contains short, canonical nouns and numerals early; this reduces generic word overlap.

4) Tighten rules for role words and inference
- Allow role nouns (goalkeeper, vendor, child) only when explicit visual evidence exists; require the caption to also include the visible evidence token (e.g., “jersey with '1'”; “pushcart with yellow umbrella”; “helmet/child seat”). Otherwise forbid roles and use neutral object+action phrases.  
- Why: prevents incorrect role inferences while still permitting high-value role tokens when visually supported.

5) Require at least one discriminative marking/equipment token for people/athletes/vehicles
- For each counted person/vehicle call out up to one compact distinguishing modifier: color, printed number/text, equipment (gloves, ball, umbrella, canopy). Encourage “red jersey with '1'” rather than “red shirt.”  
- Why: tokens like numbers and printed text are highly discriminative for CLIP.

6) Clear policy for text transcription and illegibility
- Keep “omit if illegible,” but strengthen to: “If any word/number is clearly readable, transcribe exactly (including punctuation); otherwise do not guess or approximate.” Require quoting or delimiting readable text.  
- Why: avoids hallucinated text tokens which harm alignment and correctness.

7) Require concise pose/action + one spatial relation when relevant
- Require one compact pose/action (diving, holding, jumping, riding) and at most one spatial placement (foreground/midground/background or relative: “above center person”, “to the left of sculpture”). Keep them short and adjacent to the object they modify.  
- Why: pose + spatial tokens increase CLIP match without long narratives.

8) Ban hedging and inference phrases; provide explicit prohibited words
- Forbid “appears to be,” “probably,” “someone,” “something,” “looks like a,” “maybe,” and emotional/adverbial language. Enforce affirmative, verifiable phrasing only.  
- Why: hedging introduces ambiguous tokens and reduces discriminative power.

9) Provide compact syntactic template(s) and enforce punctuation style
- Give one or two short templates (not examples of captions for images, but a sentence pattern) and insist on semicolons or commas to separate facts in the given order: [text if any]; [# + object + color/marking]; [pose/action]; [spatial]; [lighting if salient]. Specify "use numerals for counts" and "use short canonical color words."  
- Why: consistent token ordering and separators make it easier for CLIP to latch on to the discriminative tokens.

10) Provide diverse short positive & negative exemplars in the prompt (targeted, not many)
- Add 3 positive and 3 negative single-sentence exemplars showing good vs bad tradeoffs (e.g., correct use of count + color + pose vs. a generic or role-hallucinated caption). Cover sports, architecture, close-ups, small text.  
- Why: instructive exemplars are among the most effective prompt levers for frozen models.

11) Prefer short, high-information adjectives (avoid vague modifiers)
- Instruct use of concise, common color/material words (“red/white/black/wooden/metallic/cracked”) and avoid vague terms like “large,” “several,” “many,” or subjective descriptors.  
- Why: CLIP’s text encoder better matches standard color/material tokens.

12) Encourage positional ordering for CLIP alignment
- Recommend placing the highest-value facts (legible text, count+object, number/marking, color) at the very start of the sentence; follow with pose and spatial relation; end with lighting/viewpoint.  
- Why: earlier tokens typically weigh more and improve similarity.

13) Add lightweight guardrails against hallucination
- Require “if unsure, omit” policy for roles, unreadable text, and fine-grained labels (brand names, specific signage). Add explicit instruction: “Do not invent words, numbers, or logos.”  
- Why: hallucinated specific tokens can lower CLIP and SigLIP.

- Why: targeted tests reveal whether prompt changes increase discriminative tokens and improve metrics.

- Pitfall: Strong rules encourage omission instead of partial detail (model leaves out facts). Mitigation: require at least one color/marking for counted objects and enforce 2–6 facts so model must include some discriminative tokens.

_backward_through_llm:
Overall critique
- The current prompt is a good start (clear one-sentence constraint, checklist priorities) but remains too permissive and under-specified in ways that let the captioner hedge, omit high-value tokens (legible text, logos, canonical object names), or produce generic phrasing. Those weaknesses reduce CLIP image–text alignment because CLIP is sensitive to exact text/logo tokens, object counts/names, and compact spatial/action cues.

Actionable changes (what to change and why)

1. Elevate and hard-require transcription of legible text and logos
   - Why: CLIP strongly benefits from exact text/logo tokens appearing in captions.
   - How: Change the checklist so that "If any prominent text/logo is legible, transcribe the exact characters/words and give its visual position" becomes mandatory (not optional). Explicitly state: "If text/logo is legible, include exact quoted text and its location (e.g., 'Sign reads "London 2012" at top banner'). If illegible, omit."

2. Reorder the checklist into a fixed output sequence
   - Why: A predictable token order (text → counts/objects → color/material → action → spatial → lighting) helps CLIP match image features to text tokens.
   - How: Require captions to follow this canonical ordering and drop any checklist items that aren't visible. State the sentence-construction order explicitly.

3. Require numerals, canonical object names, and normalized directions
   - Why: Consistent tokens (numerals "1/2", canonical nouns "soccer ball", standard directions "left/right/foreground") increase token-repeatability across examples and CLIP alignment.
   - How: Instruct "use numerals for counts; use canonical object names from a short curated list (ball, bench, sign, bicycle, net, table, badge, brochure); use 'left/right/foreground/midground/background' for placement."

4. Replace vague placeholders ("one person") with concrete descriptors
   - Why: Generic phrases reduce specificity. CLIP benefits from specific clothing colors, accessories, and object details.
   - How: Require "number + clothing/accessory descriptors when visible" (e.g., "1 person in red jersey with number 1, wearing gloves"). Explicitly ban lone "one person" unless accompanied by clothing/accessory descriptors.

5. Make role/scene labels conditional and require evidence
   - Why: Roles (goalkeeper, vendor) boost CLIP when accurate but harm it when guessed.
   - How: Permit role words only if visually supported; require the caption to immediately follow the role with the visual evidence that justifies it (e.g., "goalkeeper (gloves, full-size goal/net behind)").

6. Force precise action/orientation wording and dynamic verbs
   - Why: Motion and orientation are discriminative for CLIP; "person diving" is less useful than "diving midair to the right toward ball."
   - How: Require dynamic verbs with orientation and, when relevant, relative direction (left/right/toward/away). Mandate midair/grounded status when visible.

7. Ban hedging, inference, and nonvisual content
   - Why: Phrases like "appears to be" or inferred emotions dilute the caption signal.
   - How: Explicitly prohibit hedging, inferred intent/emotion/role without evidence, metaphors, marketing language, and any non-image-verifiable claims.

8. Limit facts and enforce brevity with a strict word/word-range target
   - Why: Long, rambling captions include tokens that don't help CLIP and reduce clarity.
   - How: Keep the existing 2–6 facts rule but add an explicit word range (e.g., target 10–25 words) and state that exactly one sentence is required. Encourage compact phrasing of each fact.

9. Require explicit spatial relations and placement
   - Why: Relative placement (table in foreground; backdrop in background) helps CLIP anchor objects spatially.
   - How: Mandate using foreground/midground/background and left/right for at least one relation when multiple salient objects are present.

10. Insist on mentioning small but defining objects when visible
    - Why: Small objects (ball, net, badge, carving knife, brochures) are highly discriminative tokens.
    - How: Add a rule: "If small, scene-defining objects are visible and unoccluded, include them and their relation to people/furniture."

11. Provide concise positive and negative micro-examples
    - Why: Models learn behavior from examples; targeted micro-examples reduce common failure modes.
    - How: Add 6–10 one-line examples: grouped by failure mode (legible text included vs omitted; sports action vs generic diving; role justified vs unjustified). For each, show one good caption and one bad caption highlighting the exact failure.

12. Eliminate ambiguous phrases in the prompt itself
    - Why: Words like "simple spatial layout" or "if present" leave room for inconsistent behavior.
    - How: Replace vague instructions with precise rules (e.g., "include up to 6 discrete facts; each fact is a noun phrase or clause; facts must follow the canonical order").

13. Encourage use of exact punctuation for quoted text
    - Why: Including quotes around transcribed text helps CLIP tokenizers split the text clearly and keeps the transcription unambiguous.
    - How: Instruct "enclose transcribed text/logo words in double quotes and immediately state location."

14. Add an explicit prohibition on filler tokens and conjunction overload
    - Why: Excess conjunctions create noisy sentences. CLIP prefers concise token sequences.
    - How: Ask authors to use commas and semicolons sparingly and not to append unrelated adjectives or subordinate clauses.

15. Make the "2–6 discrete facts" requirement operational
    - Why: It's currently subjective; models may interpret "fact" differently.
    - How: Define what counts as a fact (e.g., "transcribed text counts as 1 fact; each object + count counts as 1; color/material modifiers do not count separately if attached to an object"). This reduces variance across outputs.

Testing and iteration guidance
- Add a held-out validation set of images where high-value tokens are known (logos, numbers, sports scenes, tools). During prompt tuning iterate until captions consistently include these tokens.
- Use quick A/B testing with the existing evaluation images to ensure revisions increase mean_clip and reduce omissions of text/logos and objects.

Why these changes will improve mean CLIP
- They force inclusion of tokens CLIP is sensitive to (exact text, logos, canonical nouns, counts, action verbs, spatial relations) and reduce filler/hedging noise that weakens text–image alignment. A fixed token order and normalized phrasing increase token-level consistency across captions, improving CLIP similarity on average.

Avoid (do not add)
- Any external reranking, verification steps, multiple-candidate outputs, JSON/tags protocol in place of single-sentence captions — these are disallowed by the evaluation constraints.

Below are concrete, actionable changes to the prompt (what to change and why) you can apply to improve CLIP image-text alignment.

Concrete feedback and suggested changes (actionable, prompt-level — not a rewrite)

1) Stronger, explicit enforcement of legible-text handling
- Problem: models often paraphrase or guess text rather than transcribing exact words, or omit partially legible text.
- Change: require quoted, exact transcription when text is clearly legible (e.g., Sign reads "SUBWAY"); explicitly instruct to preserve capitalization/punctuation as seen. If any characters are illegible, omit the transcription (no guessing).  
- Why: precise brand/text tokens strongly boost CLIP similarity; quoting reduces paraphrase variation.

2) Make the fact-ordering and separators deterministic
- Problem: loose natural-language ordering yields variability and missing priority facts.
- Change: require facts to follow the checklist order strictly (text → counts/types → color/material → pose → layout → lighting) and require semicolons as fact separators (one sentence with 2–6 semicolon-separated facts). Example instruction: "Write one sentence with 2–6 facts, separated by semicolons, in the specified priority order."  
- Why: consistent token ordering and separators reduces caption variability and makes discriminative tokens appear earlier — improves CLIP alignment.

3) Enforce canonical nouns, adjective use, and numeric format
- Problem: synonyms and vague nouns dilute discriminative tokens (e.g., “person” vs “woman in apron”).
- Change: instruct use of a short canonical style: numerals for counts ("2 people"), canonical object names (prefer "step ladder" or "extension ladder" when visible; otherwise "ladder"), and specific color/material adjectives immediately after nouns ("orange extension ladder", "timber façade"). Provide a one-line rule: "Use canonical nouns and place color/material adjectives immediately before the noun."  
- Why: canonicalization increases overlap with CLIP’s object embeddings and reduces semantic drift.

4) Require distinguishing attributes for multiple people/objects
- Problem: captions collapse people/objects into a generic count and lose discriminative details.
- Change: when count >1, require at least one distinguishing visual attribute for each person/object when visible (clothing color/type, accessory, hair, glasses) and associate it with left/right/foreground/midground where helpful. If no distinguishing attributes are visible, state only the count and location.  
- Why: adds discriminative tokens that CLIP favors (colors/accessories/positions).

5) Conservative uncertainty policy and omission rules
- Problem: hallucination of roles/intentions and guessing object identity reduces precision.
- Change: tighten uncertainty handling: "If you cannot read text or cannot visually confirm a class/attribute, omit it — do not infer. Use omission rather than hedging words ('maybe', 'appears to be')."  
- Why: reduces false tokens that hurt CLIP match quality and avoids misleading specificity.

6) Require brief internal verification heuristics (implicit)
- Problem: models sometimes output unchecked claims.
- Change: add an instruction to "internally verify" (without producing steps) before output, e.g., "Before emitting the caption, mentally verify each fact is visually supported; omit unsupported facts."  
- Why: nudges the model to apply a conservative filter; practical improvement without changing output format.

- Problem: one example set in the prompt is insufficiently diverse.
- Change: add 6–8 short pairs (good vs bad), covering: legible signage, people distinguished by clothing, ambiguous object omission, detailed material/condition (rusted/sooty), spatial layout, and lighting. Keep examples short and focused on the checklist.

- Change: tighten the prohibition: "Do not infer role/occupation, emotion, intention, or write slogans/marketing. No metaphors." Provide 1–2 counterexamples showing harmful inferences.  
- Why: keeps the caption strictly visually grounded, increasing overlap on visual tokens.

- Problem: bland material descriptions ("wall") miss discriminative tokens.
- Change: instruct to include visible surface condition adjectives when present (e.g., "paint-chipped white brick", "rusted metal roof", "sooty brick"). Ask to favor these over generic textures.

- Problem: inconsistent quoting/casing reduces exact-match potential for brand tokens.
- Change: specify how to include transcribed text (e.g., always quote exact words and preserve case/punctuation; do not translate character case).  
- Why: exact-match tokens (like brand names) align better with CLIP.

11) Small lexicon or mapping guidance (optional but helpful)
- Problem: ambiguity in object class naming leads to model choosing inconsistent synonyms.
- Change: include a compact mapping guideline: when ladder has visible rungs and fold hinge → "step ladder"; if long multi-section → "extension ladder"; when bag is clearly a backpack → "backpack" not "bag". Keep mapping short; say "prefer these canonical mappings when visually supported."  
- Why: reduces synonym noise and standardizes captions.

- Problem: no easy way to test prompt efficacy.

- Risk: being overly prescriptive (e.g., always semicolons) can produce unnatural punctuation in some languages or images; mitigate by allowing commas only if facts remain clearly separable and tokens ordered.

- Use terse, imperative sentences in the prompt ("If text is legible, transcribe it exactly and quote it." "Separate facts with semicolons, facts must follow the priority order.")

- Don’t add multi-sentence outputs, JSON, or additional verification tokens in the output — the frozen captioner expects one sentence.
- Don’t request chain-of-thought or explanatory steps in the output (internal verification nudges are fine but must not be emitted).

- Why: canonicalization increases overlap with CLIP’s object embeddings and reduces semantic drift.

4) Require distinguishing attributes for multiple people/objects
- Problem: captions collapse people/objects into a generic count and lose discriminative details.
- Change: when count >1, require at least one distinguishing visual attribute for each person/object when visible (clothing color/type, accessory, hair, glasses) and associate it with left/right/foreground/midground where helpful. If no distinguishing attributes are visible, state only the count and location.  
- Why: adds discriminative tokens that CLIP favors (colors/accessories/positions).

5) Conservative uncertainty policy and omission rules
- Problem: hallucination of roles/intentions and guessing object identity reduces precision.
- Change: tighten uncertainty handling: "If you cannot read text or cannot visually confirm a class/attribute, omit it — do not infer. Use omission rather than hedging words ('maybe', 'appears to be')."  
- Why: reduces false tokens that hurt CLIP match quality and avoids misleading specificity.

6) Require brief internal verification heuristics (implicit)
- Problem: models sometimes output unchecked claims.
- Change: add an instruction to "internally verify" (without producing steps) before output, e.g., "Before emitting the caption, mentally verify each fact is visually supported; omit unsupported facts."  
- Why: nudges the model to apply a conservative filter; practical improvement without changing output format.

7) Add concise, targeted good/bad examples that cover known failure modes
- Problem: one example set in the prompt is insufficiently diverse.
- Change: add 6–8 short pairs (good vs bad), covering: legible signage, people distinguished by clothing, ambiguous object omission, detailed material/condition (rusted/sooty), spatial layout, and lighting. Keep examples short and focused on the checklist.  
- Why: concrete contrastive examples train the model's output style and reduce generic captions.

8) Explicitly ban inference of roles, emotions, metaphors, and marketing language
- Problem: model still may output inferred roles or emotive language.
- Change: tighten the prohibition: "Do not infer role/occupation, emotion, intention, or write slogans/marketing. No metaphors." Provide 1–2 counterexamples showing harmful inferences.  
- Why: keeps the caption strictly visually grounded, increasing overlap on visual tokens.

9) Prefer discriminative surface/condition adjectives when visible
- Problem: bland material descriptions ("wall") miss discriminative tokens.
- Change: instruct to include visible surface condition adjectives when present (e.g., "paint-chipped white brick", "rusted metal roof", "sooty brick"). Ask to favor these over generic textures.  
- Why: texture/condition words are high-value tokens for CLIP matching.

10) Make punctuation/casing conventions explicit for transcribed text
- Problem: inconsistent quoting/casing reduces exact-match potential for brand tokens.
- Change: specify how to include transcribed text (e.g., always quote exact words and preserve case/punctuation; do not translate character case).  
- Why: exact-match tokens (like brand names) align better with CLIP.

11) Small lexicon or mapping guidance (optional but helpful)
- Problem: ambiguity in object class naming leads to model choosing inconsistent synonyms.
- Change: include a compact mapping guideline: when ladder has visible rungs and fold hinge → "step ladder"; if long multi-section → "extension ladder"; when bag is clearly a backpack → "backpack" not "bag". Keep mapping short; say "prefer these canonical mappings when visually supported."  
- Why: reduces synonym noise and standardizes captions.

12) Diagnostics to validate prompt changes
- Problem: no easy way to test prompt efficacy.
- Change: add simple evaluation instructions for developers: test on a held-out set emphasizing signage, multiple people, textures, and accessories; measure mean CLIP and per-category gains (text-bearing vs non-text). Iterate using targeted examples that previously performed poorly.  
- Why: targeted validation will show whether changes actually improve the objective.

Potential unintended outcomes and mitigations
- Risk: being overly prescriptive (e.g., always semicolons) can produce unnatural punctuation in some languages or images; mitigate by allowing commas only if facts remain clearly separable and tokens ordered.
- Risk: too strict omission may reduce descriptiveness in images with subtle clues; mitigate by allowing more attributes when visually supported.

Prioritization (what to change first)
1) Enforce exact transcription + quoting and case preservation. (High ROI for CLIP)
2) Require semicolon-separated facts with strict checklist order. (Reduces variance)
3) Demand distinguishing attributes for multiple people/objects. (Improves discriminability)
4) Add diverse good/bad examples that show failures found in evaluations. (Teaches style)
5) Add conservative uncertainty/omit rule and canonical noun guidance.

Why these changes will improve CLIP similarity
- CLIP scores correlate strongly with presence of specific, discriminative tokens (brand names, colors, materials, canonical object labels). The suggested edits force the captioner to emit those tokens reliably, earlier in the sentence, and in a consistent format, increasing overlap with image embeddings and reducing noisy, generic language that lowers similarity.

Implementation tips (practical wording ideas to incorporate into the prompt)
- Use terse, imperative sentences in the prompt ("If text is legible, transcribe it exactly and quote it." "Separate facts with semicolons, facts must follow the priority order.")
- Keep the canonical mapping very short — one line or bullet list.
- Provide 6 concise contrastive examples (good vs bad), each 1 sentence.

Avoid in-prompt changes that are unlikely to help
- Don’t add multi-sentence outputs, JSON, or additional verification tokens in the output — the frozen captioner expects one sentence.
- Don’t request chain-of-thought or explanatory steps in the output (internal verification nudges are fine but must not be emitted).

If you want, I can (separately) produce a short checklist of 6–8 contrastive good/bad examples and a 1‑line canonical noun mapping to plug directly into the prompt.</FEEDBACK>

text:
System:You are evaluating a captioning prompt for a frozen image captioning model.
The prompt is used to generate captions for images.
The primary objective is to improve CLIP image-text similarity.
SigLIP is reported only as a secondary diagnostic metric.

This is multimodal feedback mode.
For each low-performing example, an image-grounded critique is provided.
Use the aggregate scores and critiques to provide concise, critical feedback on how the prompt should be changed.
Do not produce captions for the examples.
Do not suggest external rerankers, verifiers, multiple candidates, tags, JSON, or non-caption protocols.

Aggregate score report:
- mean_clip: 0.330926
- mean_delta_clip: -0.001130
- clip_win_rate: 0.458333
- mean_siglip: 0.194135
- mean_delta_siglip: 0.010177

Image-grounded low-performing examples:
- image_id: flickr30k_test_016046
  image_relpath: images/flickr30k/flickr30k_test_016046.jpg
  caption: Two people stand at a wooden table with a yellow plastic basin and a bottle of orange liquid; several people sit on chairs to the right; trees and a brick wall are in the background; bright sunlight casts shadows.
  clip_score: 0.295069
  delta_clip: -0.042422
  image_grounded_critique:
    - Ask the captioner to label the scene as an outdoor demonstration/lesson when people are clearly arranged as presenters and an attentive seated audience, and describe the presenters’ actions (e.g., speaking or holding a handheld object) and the audience’s focus.
    
    - Require explicit mention of prominent objects, colors and positions (e.g., a large yellow plastic basin centered on the table, an orange liquid bottle beside it, a blue basin under the table, bag/backpack beneath).
    
    - Replace vague phrases like “several people” with concrete audience descriptions and placement (e.g., "a group of seated girls/young women on plastic chairs to the right facing the table"), and note notable clothing or pose cues for the presenters (e.g., "one wearing a blue shirt and headband, the other in a gray t‑shirt and shorts").
- image_id: flickr30k_test_013576
  image_relpath: images/flickr30k/flickr30k_test_013576.jpg
  caption: Boy rides a red toy motorcycle; jersey with "Mets" text; chain-link fence and painted wall in background; bright daylight.
  clip_score: 0.368539
  delta_clip: -0.040219
  image_grounded_critique:
    - Instruct the captioner to report the subject’s pose, expression, and gaze (e.g., a young boy smiling and looking toward the camera while seated on the toy).
    - Require specific object details for toys/vehicles (e.g., red child-sized ride-on motorcycle with flame decals, round plastic headlights and visible handlebars) rather than just “toy motorcycle.”
    - Ask for clear clothing and logo descriptions (e.g., blue Mets baseball jersey with orange script, gray sweatpants) instead of generic “jersey” mentions.
    - Ask the captioner to name the immediate setting features (asphalt playground/painted court with white lines, chain-link fence) and notable mural elements (sun, moon, globe, stick-figure children) instead of “painted wall.”

  clip_score: 0.310087
  delta_clip: -0.039361
  image_grounded_critique:
    - Add instructions to note that the scene is viewed through a glass window (mention visible reflections, the horizontal mullion/bar, and a partially obscuring American flag) so the caption distinguishes interior vs. exterior visual layers.
    - Ask the model to name salient subject attributes and actions (e.g., "older woman with white hair wearing a white blouse, seated at a table, looking into or handling a bag") rather than just "a woman."
    - Require explicit mention of prominent, legible object details and placement (e.g., a front-facing red shopping bag with readable "American Girl Place" text placed on the table/edge) and nearby foreground elements (green foliage at lower right).

  image_relpath: images/flickr30k/flickr30k_test_029272.jpg

  delta_clip: -0.036965
  image_grounded_critique:

    - Call out salient audience reactions and spatial relationships: describe the open‑mouthed, astonished boy at the front left, the children seated at the stage edge, and standing adults behind him rather than lumping them as “several spectators.”
    - Add specific, discriminative clothing and accessory details: note dreadlocks pulled back, colored sneakers and wristbands, and the performer’s black shirt and baggy gray sweatpants as visually distinctive elements.

    - Emphasize riverside architecture and signage: describe stilted shopfronts, corrugated roofs/awnings and colorful facades along the bank, and transcribe any clearly readable signs or lettering.

The feedback should target reusable prompt changes, not example-specific captions.
Query: Produce exactly one concise caption (one sentence) that states only visually verifiable facts. Include 2–6 discrete visual facts drawn from this checklist in the given priority order when present: 1) legible text: transcribe exact words; 2) counts and object types (e.g., "2 people", "one bicycle"); 3) key color/material/texture for those objects (e.g., "orange backpack", "wooden façade"); 4) pose/action/orientation (e.g., "person seen from behind walking away; holding two poles"); 5) simple spatial layout (foreground / midground / background placement); 6) lighting/viewpoint/occlusion cues (e.g., "bright sunlight casting long shadows", "elevated vantage; tree partially obscures façade"). Use canonical object names and exact counts, standard direction words (left/right/foreground/background), and numerals or short words for numbers. Do not infer roles, emotions, intentions, or use metaphors, slogans, or marketing language (avoid "farmer", "happy", "adventure", etc.). If text is not clearly legible, omit it rather than guess. Keep the caption factual, compact, and limited to one sentence containing 2–6 concrete facts—no lists, tags, extra sentences, or commentary. Example (good): "Sign reads 'Outdoor World'; two adults walk toward the store entrance; timber façade and concrete forecourt; overcast sky." Counterexample (bad): "A happy farmer enjoys a sunny day in the countryside."
Response: Overall assessment: captions are too generic and often omit discriminative, image-grounded details that improve CLIP similarity. Use the following concise, reusable prompt edits to force more precise, verifiable visual facts and reduce vague phrasing.

Recommended prompt changes

1) Enforce strict concreteness and counts
- Require numeric counts for visible instances (use digits) instead of vague words like “several” or “many.” If a count is unclear, prefer “group” only with an approximate modifier (avoid when possible).

2) Prioritize and require discriminative object attributes
- For each counted object, require at least one distinguishing attribute when visible (color, material, pattern, logo/text, or distinctive part). E.g., “red plastic basin,” “wooden skiff,” “blue Mets jersey with orange script.”

3) Strengthen pose/action and gaze as mandatory when clearly visible
- If people are performing an action or have a clear gaze/pose, require one concise verb or orientation (e.g., “standing and speaking,” “smiling and looking toward camera,” “mid‑jump with bent knees”). Do not infer intent/emotion.

4) Transcribe legible text strictly and place it
- Make legible text transcription mandatory when characters are clearly readable; include exact text in quotes and indicate approximate placement (e.g., “Sign reads 'DUNG ANH...' on riverbank”).

5) Call out visual layers and occlusion
- If reflections, glass, mullions, shadows, or partial occlusion are visible, require a short note (e.g., “viewed through glass with reflections,” “foreground foliage partially obscures table”).

6) Prefer specific, canonical object names and toy/vehicle part details
- Replace generic nouns with specific types and visible parts (e.g., “ride-on motorcycle with plastic headlight and handlebars,” “narrow wooden skiff,” “chain-link fence with painted mural”).

7) Avoid unsupported role inference — but allow explicit “scene label” only when multiple strong cues exist
- Do not infer roles/emotions by default. Permit a short scene-type label (e.g., “outdoor demonstration/lesson”) only if several clear visual cues co-occur (presenters facing seated audience, table with materials, microphone, audience orientation). Require the caption to also list the concrete visual cues that justify the label.

8) Tighten factual count of facts and brevity constraints
- Keep 2–6 facts as required; explicitly mandate that each fact be a visually verifiable clause (counts/objects, attribute, pose, spatial relation, lighting). Discourage filler adjectives and high-level summaries.

9) Give explicit forbids and replacements
- Forbid vague qualifiers (“several,” “group of people,” “a lot”) and generic role words (“people in front”) unless replaced by specific count/location. Replace “wearing a jersey” with “blue Mets jersey with orange script” only when the logo/wording is visible.

10) Add short diagnostics to training prompts (not to end-user captions)
- During model generation, include an internal checklist verify step: (A) did you transcribe readable text? (B) did you include counts where visible? (C) did you add at least one discriminative attribute? If any are false but present in image, force re-generation.

Rationale in one line: More precise counts, colors/materials, pose/gaze, exact text, and explicit occlusion/layer cues produce more discriminative captions that better align with CLIP’s image-text similarity.

   - Ask for short spatial relations when relevant (e.g., “ball airborne near outstretched hands,” “bag resting on table in foreground,” “flag hanging in background”), using foreground/midground/background terms.

   - Instruct to mention visible tools/accessories/material condition when present (e.g., gloves, net, knife/chisel, wood shavings, wet coat, reflection), because these improve text–image alignment.

   - Explicitly ban role/emotion/intent inference or generic labels that aren’t visually verifiable (no “goalkeeper,” “happy,” “working”), and require omission rather than guessing for unclear text or ambiguous items.

7. Enforce the one‑sentence, 2–6‑fact, concise output format
   - Reiterate: exactly one sentence, 2–6 discrete facts drawn from the checklist, no extra commentary. Add a soft length constraint (for example: prefer ≤30 words) to reduce verbosity that dilutes CLIP signal.

   - Before output, check that the caption: (a) contains only one sentence, (b) includes 2–6 facts from the checklist in priority order, (c) uses canonical names and numerals, (d) omits uncertain text/roles.

Implementing these changes will make captions denser in the specific visual cues CLIP relies on (text, counts, colors/materials, tools/actions, spatial relations), reduce vague phrasing, and keep outputs compact and verifiable.

High-level summary
- The current prompt has many of the right constraints (one sentence, 2–6 facts, checklist priorities) but is too loose in execution: it allows vague nouns, soft ordering, and no machine-checkable rules. That lets the generator produce safe but CLIP-weak captions (generic phrasing, missing small objects/text/tools, weak spatial relations). To improve mean CLIP similarity, tighten the constraints, make priority enforcement explicit and machine-enforceable, force more diagnostic tokens (text, exact counts, canonical object names, colors, tools, spatial relations), and add simple validation checks plus targeted examples/anti‑examples.

Concrete feedback and change directions (actionable, reusable)

1. Enforce checklist priority and clause ordering
- Problem: The prompt describes priorities but does not force order; generators may ignore lower-priority but discriminative cues.
- Change method: Require that facts, if present, appear in strict priority order (text first, counts/types next, attributes, action/orientation, layout, lighting/occlusion). If a fact is absent, skip but maintain ordering of remaining facts.
- Rationale: CLIP benefits most from certain tokens (exact words, object counts, colors) appearing early; deterministic ordering increases model attention to these features.

2. Make transcription rules exact and machine-checkable
- Problem: “legible text” guidance is ambiguous and optional.
- Change method: Require that any transcribed text appears as an exact quoted substring and as the first clause. If text is not clearly legible, require explicit omission (“no legible text” should not be stated — instead simply omit transcription).
- Rationale: Exact transcription tokens strongly improve alignment; forcing quotes prevents paraphrase/hallucination.

3. Mandate canonical object names and numerals
- Problem: Vague or non-canonical nouns (“one person”) reduce CLIP signal.
- Change method: Demand canonical object names (people -> “person”; vehicles -> “car/bicycle”) and numerals (1, 2, 3). Provide a short canonical-name mapping (or examples) in the prompt to guide choices.
- Rationale: CLIP similarity improves when captions use common nouns that map to visual concepts.

4. Require explicit, concrete attributes (color/material/texture) for counted objects
- Problem: Attributes are often omitted or generic.
- Change method: For each counted object, require at least one visible attribute (color, material, pattern) when it is clearly present. Formally: for N objects listed, include attribute tokens for ≥1 of them.
- Rationale: Color and material words are high-signal for image-text models.

5. Force actionable, directional verbs for actions/poses
- Problem: Passive or vague verbs (“one person is diving across”) are less informative.
- Change method: Require active verb + orientation/direction (e.g., “diving to the right, arms extended”), and when hands interact with an object, require naming the tool or the hand action (carving with chisel; holding a bag). Provide a short preferred-verb list to encourage specific verbs (walks, runs, holds, carries, sits, leans, tosses, reflects).
- Rationale: Action verbs with direction increase discriminative alignment.

- Problem: Spatial language is inconsistent.
- Change method: Require at least one spatial relation when multiple objects are described (e.g., “X in foreground, Y in background,” or “ball near outstretched hands”).
- Rationale: Spatial terms anchor tokens to image layout, improving CLIP alignment.

- Problem: Small but diagnostic items (gloves, nets, chisel, wood shavings, reflections) are often missed.
- Change method: Add an explicit rule: if a small tool/accessory is visually near a person’s hands or on a nearby surface, include it as one of the 2–6 facts. If a reflective surface creates a visible reflection of an object/person, include “reflection” as a fact.
- Rationale: These tokens are high-value for alignment.

- Problem: Model sometimes infers roles/intentions (goalkeeper, seller) or guesses illegible text.
- Change method: Explicitly forbid role/emotion inference and require omission of any fact not directly verifiable. Provide a short “uncertainty” rule: if the model must guess >30% of a fact (e.g., gender, occupation, illegible text), omit it.
- Rationale: Hallucinated facts degrade CLIP alignment with the image.

9. Machine‑verifiable output constraints (automatic validation rules)
- Problem: The prompt relies on the model to self-check but there’s no mechanical verification.
- Change method: Add explicit validation steps the generator must run before output:
  - Single sentence only (no internal periods except for acronyms).
  - Contains 2–6 comma/semicolon-separated facts.
  - If transcription present, must be in quotes and appear first.

  - Word count soft cap (<=30 words) to avoid dilution.

- Problem: The model needs concrete guidance on phrasing, punctuation, and priority.
- Change method: Add 3 concise positive examples and 3 negative counterexamples that illustrate the priority order, use of quotes for text, canonical names, and omission of inferences. Keep examples short and tightly aligned to the rules.
- Rationale: Examples dramatically help alignment and reduce interpretation errors.

- Problem: Long prose buries facts.

- Problem: Over-strict rules can make the model omit too much or produce very terse captions.

"1 person holds a red umbrella; wooden bench in foreground; wet pavement reflecting streetlights."

"A happy farmer enjoys a sunny day in the countryside."

_backward_through_llm:
High-level summary
- The current instruction is directionally good but too permissive and non-normative in places; that lets the frozen captioner fall back to generic text and miss discriminative signals (legible text/logos, numbers, unique colors, pose, occlusion) that raise CLIP alignment.
- Make the rules prescriptive and enforceable: force a canonical ordering, explicit transcription rules, concrete noun usage, and clear fallbacks for uncertainty. Also tighten length/wording constraints so outputs stay compact and focused.

Concrete, actionable feedback to change the prompt (each item is a single recommended edit you can apply)
1) Make the priority ordering normative and syntactic
   - Require that, when legible text/logos/numbers are present, they must appear first in the sentence, in quotes, e.g. "Sign reads 'X'", then follow with remaining facts in the required order.
   - Rationale: positioning text first makes captions align to the strongest CLIP signal and avoids it being dropped or paraphrased.

2) Enforce exact transcription rules
   - Explicitly instruct: transcribe only clearly legible characters, put them in double quotes, do not guess, and omit text when not legible.
   - Rationale: exact quoted text maps strongly to image embeddings and prevents hallucinated words that harm similarity.

3) Define "facts" and enforce 2–6 facts with a strict interpretation
   - Define a fact as a discrete visual assertion (legible text; count+object; color/texture of that object; pose/action; one spatial placement; one lighting/occlusion cue).
   - Require outputs to contain between 2 and 6 such facts and instruct the model to stop once 6 facts are reached.
   - Rationale: reduces rambling/generic captions and focuses on discriminative tokens.

4) Require canonical object names and numerals
   - Instruct use of canonical nouns (e.g., "dog", "bicycle", "store sign", "table") and numerals (use "2" not "two"), and require at least one canonical object be named.
   - Rationale: concrete nouns and numerals are high-signal for CLIP.

5) Ban vague terms and inference
   - Explicitly ban single-word generics ("sign", "object", "thing") without a qualifying noun or transcription; ban role/emotion/intent inferences ("happy", "volunteer", "customer") and hedges ("appears", "seems").
   - Rationale: prevents low-value filler and hallucinated semantics that reduce alignment.

6) Require at least one high-priority discriminative attribute when present
   - If legible text exists, include it; otherwise require at least one of: distinctive color, unique shape/graphic, readable number/date, or clear pose/action to be included before adding lower-priority facts.
   - Rationale: pushes the model to pick the highest-CLIP-value signal.

7) Give explicit fallback rules for uncertainty
   - If count cannot be determined confidently, use safe positional phrasing ("foreground person", "a pair near the entrance") instead of wrong numerals.
   - If color is ambiguous, prefer neutral but descriptive wording ("dark jacket" rather than "black jacket") or omit.
   - Rationale: reduces false precise claims, which harm alignment more than conservative phrases.

8) Enforce single-sentence, comma-separated structure and concise length
   - State that the caption must be exactly one sentence, facts separated by commas, and target a short length (e.g., aim for 8–20 words or at most X tokens) while still satisfying 2–6 facts.
   - Rationale: minimizes extraneous language and keeps captions dense in CLIP-relevant tokens.

9) Require spatial or occlusion cue for at least one key object
   - Instruct inclusion of one placement clause (foreground/midground/background) or single occlusion/reflection phrase when it affects visibility.
   - Rationale: spatial words often drive image-text alignment and resolve ambiguity.

10) Give concrete micro-guidelines for phrasing patterns to prefer
   - Examples: "Sign reads 'X'"; "2 people in foreground"; "red shopping bag at left of table"; "dog with brown patch on rump walking left"; "seen through glass with reflection".
   - Rationale: modeling a few stable syntactic templates reduces model variance and discourages generic outputs.

11) Provide a short set of bad examples to ban repetition patterns
   - Show 2–3 counterexamples that illustrate common failures (generic descriptions, inferred emotions, invented text) and state that similar language is prohibited.
   - Rationale: negative examples are effective at removing fallback habits.

12) Encourage mentioning wearable/readable small items when visible
   - Explicitly require transcription of readable text on small items (lanyard badges, bag logos, newspapers) and color/shape of small but discriminative objects (collar, lanyard color).
   - Rationale: small labeled items often produce strong CLIP matches.

13) Decoder/generation bias guidance (within prompt)
   - Instruct the generator to prioritize inclusion of "text or color or number" tokens when any such item is detected; e.g., "if any legible alphanumeric characters are visible, include them first; otherwise include a dominant color term for a key object."
   - Rationale: nudges the frozen model to choose higher-utility tokens during generation.

14) Clarify edge cases and tie-breakers
   - Specify which fact types to drop first if the 6-fact limit is reached (drop the least discriminative: extra adjectives > secondary spatial items > extra lighting words).
   - Rationale: ensures a consistent preference for higher-CLIP facts.

Why these changes will improve CLIP alignment
- CLIP prefers exact words that correspond to visible, discriminative tokens (logos, numbers, unique colors, canonical nouns). Making transcription first and forcing inclusion of such items increases overlap with CLIP text tokens.
